question: Move the AED at P.S. 146 Ann M. Short into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 146 Ann M. Short (School, ZIP 10029) has a registered AED at "FRONT ENTRANCE BY SCHOOL SAFETY".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.18 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 9 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 7 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists The Mount Sinai Hospital, a hospital normally staffed around the clock, 337 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving the AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a real gap in coverage. The school currently reaches only 55 of 168 hours weekly during the school year and zero hours in summer [E2, E3], yet the area expects 1.18 cardiac-arrest calls annually during times when every nearby AED is closed [E4]. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED reaches 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without it [E7]. The seven other AEDs within 400 meters are all closed after hours [E5], so this location could meaningfully improve access when it matters most.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate identifies a real coverage gap, but the case for moving this specific AED remains uncertain. Yes, the school reaches only 55 of 168 hours weekly [E2, E3], and 1.18 calls yearly occur when nearby AEDs are closed [E4]. However, we don't know the actual locations of those calls within the ZIP code [E9]—they may not be near this school at all. Mount Sinai Hospital sits just 337 meters away and is staffed 24/7 [E8], potentially offering a better host. We also lack critical data: cabinet costs, vandalism risk, whether the school permits after-hours access [E9], and whether moving versus installing elsewhere would yield more lives saved. Before committing resources here, we should evaluate whether Mount Sinai or another existing facility could serve this gap more efficiently.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic correctly notes we lack the precise call locations within the ZIP code [E9], which matters. However, the 1.18 annual calls occurring during closed-AED hours [E4] represent real cardiac arrests in this school's two-minute walking area—the geographic unit designed to capture meaningful response distance. Mount Sinai at 337 meters [E8] is indeed closer than some points, but it's a hospital, not a public street-accessible location. The skeptic's suggestion to evaluate Mount Sinai first is reasonable, but that evaluation should happen in parallel with this proposal, not instead of it. A street-wall cabinet at P.S. 146 would guarantee public 24/7 access regardless of hospital policies or staffing changes.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate makes a fair point that Mount Sinai's hospital status may limit public access compared to a street-wall cabinet. But we still face a critical gap: we don't know whether those 1.18 annual calls [E4] actually occur near P.S. 146 or elsewhere in the ZIP code [E9]. Installing a cabinet here could miss the real problem area entirely. Before spending on this specific location, the city should map where those closed-AED-hour calls actually happened and whether Mount Sinai or another existing 24/7 facility could serve them. That targeting matters more than speed of installation.

verdict.summary: Real coverage gap exists (1.18 annual calls during closed-AED hours [E4]), but precise call locations within ZIP unknown [E9]. Mount Sinai alternative at 337m [E8] requires evaluation before committing to P.S. 146 relocation.
verdict.strongestFor: School reaches only 55/168 weekly hours [E2, E3]; 66.5% survival with public AED versus 43.0% without [E7]; seven nearby AEDs all closed after-hours [E5].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Actual 2025 call locations unknown within ZIP code [E9]; Mount Sinai Hospital 337m away staffed 24/7 [E8]; cabinet cost, vandalism risk, school access policies unknown [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Map exact locations of 1.18 annual closed-AED-hour calls [E4]; assess Mount Sinai 24/7 public AED feasibility [E8]; then compare cost-effectiveness of P.S. 146 cabinet versus alternatives.
